text: Tivoli Gardens, also known as Tivoli (Danish pronunciation: [ˈtsʰiwoli]), is an amusement park and pleasure garden located in downtown Copenhagen, Denmark, next to the Central rail station. It opened on 15 August 1843 and is the second-oldest operating amusement park in the world, after Dyrehavsbakken in nearby Klampenborg, both in Denmark. With 4.25 million visitors in 2024, Tivoli is the most visited amusement park in Scandinavia and the second-most popular seasonal amusement park in the world, behind Europa-Park. It is also the fifth-most visited amusement park in Europe, ranking after Disneyland Park, Efteling, Europa-Park, and Walt Disney Studios Park. Originally named "Tivoli & Vauxhall," the park's name references the Jardin de Tivoli in Paris (named after Tivoli near Rome, Italy) and Vauxhall Gardens in London. The park was founded by Georg Carstensen (b. 1812 – d. 1857), who obtained a five-year charter from King Christian VIII by stating that "when the people are amusing themselves, they do not think about politics," and was granted use of approximately 15 acres (61,000 m²) of the fortified glacis outside Vesterport (the West Gate) for an annual rent. Until the 1850s, Tivoli was outside the city, accessible only through Vesterport. From its inception, it featured exotic-style buildings, a theatre, band stands, restaurants, cafés, flower gardens, mechanical rides like a merry-go-round and a primitive scenic railway, and nighttime illumination with colored lamps and fireworks reflected in its lake. Composer Hans Christian Lumbye (b. 1810 – d. 1874) served as musical director from 1843 to 1872, inspired by Viennese waltz composers such as the Strauss family, and became known as the "Strauss of the North"; many of his compositions, including "Salute to the Ticket Holders of Tivoli," "Carnival Joys," and "A Festive Night at Tivoli," are specifically inspired by the gardens and are still performed by the Tivoli Symphony Orchestra. In 1874, a Chinese-style Pantomimeteatret (pantomime theatre) replaced an older smaller theatre, with an open audience stand and a mechanical peacock's tail curtain operated by five men. The theatre has long been the home of Italian pantomimes introduced by Giuseppe Casorti, based on the Commedia dell'Arte tradition, featuring characters Cassander, Columbine, Harlequin, and Pierrot, with no spoken dialogue, a feature that supports its international appeal. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Tivoli hosted human exhibitions. In 1943, Nazi sympathizers burned many of its buildings, including the concert hall, to the ground, and temporary structures were built, with the park reopening after a few weeks. In June 1944, during the World War II occupation, sabotage attacks damaged sections of Rutschebanen, and the government prioritized restoring operations, leading to the renovation and reopening of Rutschebanen just 25 days later. Tivoli continues to evolve while preserving its original charm and traditions; Georg Carstensen stated in 1844 that "Tivoli will never, so to speak, be finished," a sentiment echoed by Walt Disney when describing Disneyland. In Danish, Icelandic, Norwegian, and Swedish, the word tivoli is now synonymous with any amusement park. The park is best known for its wooden roller coaster, Rutschebanen (also called Bjergbanen, or The Mountain Coaster), built in 1914, which is one of the world's oldest operating wooden roller coasters and an ACE Coaster Classic. An operator controls the ride by braking to limit speed during descents. Another roller coaster, Dæmonen (The Demon), includes an Immelmann loop, a vertical loop, and a zero-G roll, lasting one minute and forty-six seconds, and was built after the removal of the older Slangen (The Snake) ride. In 2017, a virtual reality experience was added to Dæmonen, simulating a flight through ancient China with encounters with dragons and demons. Dæmonen is located next to the concert hall. The Star Flyer, a 260-foot (80-meter) high swing ride built by Funtime, opened in 2006 and offers panoramic city views. On 1 May 2009, Vertigo, a looping plane ride where riders control the plane, opened but had extremely low capacity and significant downtime, and was removed in 2021. On 11 April 2013, the Zamperla Air Race ride Aquila opened, a giant swing and spinner with centrifugal forces up to 4 g, named after the Eagle constellation. Newer attractions include Fatamorgana, opened in 2016, the world's first Condor 2GH, offering two seating options—one milder with two-seater gondolas and a thrilling version with riders slung at high speed in a ring facing away from the center—and Tik Tak, opened in 2018, the first permanent installation of a Mondial Shake R5, slightly less aggressive than the traveling model and highly themed. Tivoli hosts a Halloween Fest in October and Christmas Holidays in December, and during summer, features fireworks shows every Saturday. In 2022, the firework season ran from June 4 to September 24, with shows held on the roof of the Concert Hall to the music of Gioachino Rossini's The Barber of Seville. The Nimb Hotel is the only hotel located on-site, while the Tivoli Hotel & Congress Centre shares only a name with the park, maintaining close cooperation. Many interior designs were created by Thomas Winkler, chief artist at Tivoli Gardens since 2009. The park serves as a venue for performing arts and is an active part of Copenhagen’s cultural scene. The Tivoli Concert Hall hosts classical concerts featuring international music legends. The Pantomime Theatre, designed by Vilhelm Dahlerup (also known for the Royal Danish Theatre), is a toy-like historicist Chinese-style building with a mechanical peacock's tail curtain operated by five men and is primarily used for pantomime theatre in the Italian commedia dell'arte tradition, performed daily with a live pit orchestra, and also hosts ballet and modern dance by choreographers such as August Bournonville, Dinna Bjørn, Louise Midjord, and Paul James Rooney. The Tivoli Youth Guard, founded in 1844, consists of boys and girls aged 8–16 in uniforms resembling the Royal Danish Guard, complete with bearskins, and performs concerts, participates in parades, stands guard at monuments during special events, and represents the park at various functions. During warmer months, Tivoli features a live music series called Fredagsrock (Friday Rock), which has previously included acts such as Roxette, the Smashing Pumpkins, Sting, the Beach Boys, Pet Shop Boys, Kanye West, 5 Seconds of Summer, and Danish acts like TV-2, Nephew, Hanne Boel, Raveonettes, and Thomas Helmig. Tivoli Gardens also serves as a venue during the Copenhagen Jazz Festival.
